query: Explain the difference between `git merge` and `git rebase` in two short paragraphs, with one sentence on when to prefer each.
result:
`git merge` joins two branches by creating a new merge commit whose two parents are the tips of each branch. Every existing commit stays exactly as it was, so the history records that parallel work happened and when it came together. That makes merge non-destructive and safe on shared branches, but the log can fill with merge commits and branching lines that are harder to read.

`git rebase` takes the commits from your branch and replays them one by one on top of another branch. Each replayed commit gets a new hash, and you end up with a straight, linear history, as if you had started your work from the latest upstream commit. That history is easier to read and bisect, but because rebase rewrites commits, anyone who already pulled the old ones will run into conflicts.

**When to prefer each:** Rebase to tidy up your own local or unpushed feature branch before you share it, and merge to integrate work on branches other people already use, such as `main`.
